title: Helping Others Finish What They Can’t
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post retells the 1992 Barcelona Olympics moment when sprinter Derek Redmond tore a hamstring mid-race and his father came onto the track to help him limp to the finish. From it the author draws a leadership lesson: great leaders, like great parents and coaches, help others complete what they cannot finish alone. Good leaders hang back at first and step in when their position, influence, or expertise can close the gap. The author lists the kinds of help this can involve, from closing deals and navigating politics to meeting deadlines. The father's letting go a few feet from the line models support that still lets the person finish on their own. A note on Jim Redmond carrying the torch in 2012 ends the piece.
points: Leaders earn their keep by stepping in to help people finish what they cannot complete alone, as the Redmond story shows.
The best help starts from a distance and moves in only when the leader's position, influence or expertise is needed.
The support can be concrete: closing deals, delivering hard pitches, securing resources, resolving conflicts, or simply working beside someone to hit a deadline.
Jim Redmond releasing his son before the line illustrates helping without taking over the achievement.
quotes: Midway through the race, Derek Redmond tore his hamstring and fell to his knees on the track. Wincing in pain, he eventually stood and then began limping to finish the race.

His father, Jim Redmond, who had always been his biggest fan, was in the stands watching this misfortune unfold. Once his son collapsed, he quickly pushed his way through security to be with him on the track.
After a hug, Jim Redmond put his son’s arm around his shoulder and said, “I’m here. We’ll finish this together.” And together they limped and walked toward the finish line.
A few feet from the line, Jim let go of his son so Derek could cross on his own. The father and son team received a standing ovation from the crowd.

They stand ready to help from a distance, and then move in when their position, influence, physicality, or expertise can help them finish the job. In some cases, leaders just show up and get busy working when a team member’s deadline can’t be met without their assistance.
When needed, they go out of their way to extend a hand to pull people over the finish line. Just like Jim Redmond did that fateful day.
